task:
Investigate why the Dispatch service can acknowledge success before its audit event is durable. Identify all affected handlers and explain each mechanism from original evidence. Handlers with no audit action are outside scope. Distinguish safe counterexamples. This is an authored, read-only fixture, not a reproduced incident.

Primitive contracts: appendCommitted resolves only after durable storage and rejects on failure; appendCommittedSync returns only after durable storage and throws on failure; commitOutbox atomically commits all events durably before resolving. Returning a successful response or calling response.send makes it observable immediately; later awaits cannot retract it. Process termination loses memory, microtasks, and timers. Business primitives updateEntity/charge/render/query do not record audit events.

Environment input is ALREADY LOADED: state.records maps all 20 handler paths to COMPLETE source text, including imports. state.refs maps each path to versioned block references. state.contracts is the full contracts.ts text. This is input preparation, not model analysis. Do not rediscover or print inventories, symbols, lengths, or all handler bodies.

Use this semantic-computation protocol:
1. Your FIRST code action should use jev.map(state.records, genericQuestions, state.contracts). Write one or two generic questions to identify audit-relevant handlers and missing helper context. Map applies each question to EACH record. Print a compact ID/probability table, not full result objects. Keep null/unknown explicit.
2. Select candidates using the results. In code, follow their actual imports and load needed helper definitions with repo tools into external state. Do not print the helper bodies yet. Missing helper behavior remains unresolved regardless of a high score. Keep ordinary search/read available for recovery.
3. Use a SECOND semantic pass to judge early acknowledgement with that context. Use jev.map(selectedRecords, {early:{type:'noul',instructions:'<your complete generic criterion for this handler>'}}, helperContext). Shared helpers/contracts go in the THIRD argument, never as extra records to classify. You may instead compose per-record context bundles. Print compact decisions only.
4. Based on those results, print NUMBERED original source chains for suspected problems and plausible safe counterexamples. Read to resolve a concrete question; avoid rereading every irrelevant record. Distinguish what was loaded into state from what you actually saw printed. Budget is 14,000 printed characters total; use about 2,000 for screening/routing and reserve the rest for decisive evidence. Stop retrying output that cannot fit.
5. Deliver JSON: findings:[{path,mechanism,evidence:['path:start-end',...]}], ruled_out:[{path,why}], limitations:[...]. Cite actual numbered lines, never estimated offsets. Root makes the final assessment. Explicitly state unresolved evidence.

The choice of questions, candidate selection, dependency composition, second-pass judgments, source review and final answer are yours. The host only preloads input, binds questions and packs API requests.

README.md.text:
# Dispatch service

This is an authored, read-only investigation fixture. No infrastructure runs here.
Each exported function under handlers/ is an independent HTTP handler.
Handlers return response objects, except files.ts, which uses a response sender.
Audit helper implementations live under services/.
The external storage and response primitives are specified in contracts.ts.
A process may terminate at any instruction; in-memory work and timers are lost.
A successful HTTP response is observable when a handler returns it or calls response.send().
Only a durable audit record (including an audit record in a committed outbox) satisfies the audit requirement.

auditRelevant.instructions: For this handler record, using the shared contracts, does the handler attempt to record an audit event? Count direct calls to appendCommitted, appendCommittedSync, or commitOutbox, and also indirect audit recording via an imported helper whose name or call-site comments indicate audit/outbox persistence. Business primitives updateEntity, charge, render, and query do not record audit events. Handlers with no audit action are not audit-relevant. Answer yes only if an audit action is present or clearly delegated.

missingHelper.instructions: For this handler record, using the shared contracts, is the relative order of a successful observable response and durable audit storage impossible to decide from this file alone because the audit write, the response, or both are delegated to an imported helper whose function body is not in this record? Answer yes if a missing helper definition is required. Answer no if the handler has no audit action, or if both the response and the audit durability are fully visible in this record plus the contracts.

early.instructions: For this handler, using the shared contracts and helper definitions: can a successful response become observable before the handler's audit event is durably stored? Contracts: appendCommitted resolves only after durable storage and rejects on failure; appendCommittedSync returns only after durable storage and throws on failure; commitOutbox atomically commits all events durably before resolving. Returning a successful response or calling response.send makes success observable immediately; later awaits cannot retract it. Process termination loses memory, microtasks, and timers. updateEntity/charge/render/query do not record audit events. Count audit only if this handler or a helper it calls actually records an audit/outbox event. Answer yes if success can be observed while the audit write is not yet durable: response before await of appendCommitted/commitOutbox; fire-and-forget promise; void/unawaited call; timer, microtask, queue, or retry buffer that returns before durable commit; catch that still returns success after audit rejection; or a helper that schedules audit after returning. Answer no if the handler has no audit action, or success is returned only after durable appendCommitted/appendCommittedSync/commitOutbox, including when a helper awaits that primitive before returning and the handler awaits the helper before responding. A later failure that prevents the response is not early acknowledgement.

findings.mechanism: Handler awaits schedule then returns 200, but schedule only registers a 250ms timer and returns. record/appendCommitted runs later inside that timer; rejection is swallowed. The response is therefore observable while the audit event is still only a timer callback. Process termination drops the timer before durability.
response.send emits status 200 before await record. send is immediately observable and a later await cannot retract it. Termination before appendCommitted resolves loses the in-flight audit write.

Handler awaits publish then returns 202. publish only pushes the event onto an in-memory pending array and returns. Durable record happens only in drain, and a repo search finds drain solely at its definition in services/bus.ts — nothing on this request path calls it. Success is observable with the audit event only in memory.

On the success path attempt awaits record before the handler returns 200. On failure, attempt catches appendCommitted rejection and returns normally, so preferences still returns 200. Success can therefore be observed when the audit event was not stored.

Handler awaits submit then returns 202. submit only stores the event in an in-memory Map and queues flush on a microtask; it does not await record. flush later calls record and swallows errors. Response is observable before durability; termination drops the Map and microtask.
void record starts appendCommitted without awaiting it, then the handler returns 202. The successful response is observable before the promise settles; termination loses that in-flight write.

ruled_out.why: Safe counterexample. Promise.all awaits both charge and record, and record awaits appendCommitted, before the 201 return (handlers/billing.ts:3-5, services/journal.ts:2-4). A record rejection prevents the response.
Safe counterexample. deliver awaits record before returning the receipt; the handler awaits deliver before returning 202 (handlers/delivery.ts:3-5, services/dispatch.ts:3-5, services/journal.ts:2-4).

Safe counterexample despite pass2 probability 0.39. withRetry awaits record and, on rejection, awaits record again; a second rejection propagates, so enrollment returns 201 only after a successful durable append (handlers/enrollment.ts:3-5, services/retry.ts:3-8, services/journal.ts:2-4).
Safe counterexample. await record completes appendCommitted before the 200 return (handlers/profile.ts:3-6, services/journal.ts:2-4).
Safe counterexample. enqueue awaits commitOutbox before resolving; the handler awaits enqueue before returning 202 (handlers/retention.ts:3-5, services/outbox.ts:2-4).
Safe counterexample. recordSync calls appendCommittedSync, which returns only after durable storage and throws on failure, before the 201 return (handlers/sessions.ts:3-5, services/journal.ts:5-7).

limitations: Unresolved: handlers/assets.ts, handlers/catalog.ts, handlers/health.ts, handlers/locale.ts, handlers/metrics.ts, handlers/preview.ts, handlers/search.ts, and handlers/version.ts were only pass1-scored as not audit-relevant (probabilities about 0.03-0.05) and were not printed. If they have no audit action they are outside scope; absence of an audit call is not line-verified.
